summary: Intermittent 429 waves after priority-label migration + nginx proxy affinity
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports repeated 429 waves across many short-lived websocket and HTTP streams after a recent priority-label migration and a change to nginx upstream affinity on their dedicated pool. Impact: ~15% of live inference calls rejected with 429 for 10-30s windows, causing degraded UX in their realtime feature. No invoice/billing impact reported.

Environment: Dedicated pool in prod-us-west, customer on committed capacity, traffic pattern is a mix of long-lived websockets (chat sessions) and high-rate batch embedding uploads. Priority labels were remapped yesterday (2026-03-09) as part of a tenant reclassification rollout coordinated with the customer. Edge proxy (nginx) affinity was turned on at the same time for sticky upstreams to improve cache hit rates.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Customer runs an orchestrated test: 200 parallel websocket session starts over 90s, each sending short messages leading to many small token-generation streams.
2) Simultaneously trigger 8 concurrent batch embedding uploads from the same tenant using different API keys.
3) Observe rate-limit responses / 429s emitted by API gateway and edge-proxy logs.

Observed behavior:
- 429 responses appear in waves correlated to nginx upstream connection rebalances every ~20s.
- Rate limiter telemetry shows rapid token-window depletion on tenant quota with sudden refill gaps.
- Some long-lived websocket sessions received 429 mid-stream and clients had to reconnect.
- Console shows temporary spike in per-route rejection counts while tenant-level counters stayed near expected.

Expected behavior: No client-visible 429s for customers within their committed throughput during short upstream rebalances; system should gracefully queue or fallback to compatible model variant rather than failing.

Initial logs & metrics observed:
- api-gateway logs: repeated 429 with reason header "quota_window_exhausted" and x-rate-reset intervals aligning with nginx drain windows.
- edge-proxy (nginx) logs: upstream connection reassignments to different origin pods with 502/504 spikes suppressed but connection reset metrics rising.
- rate-limiter internal metrics: token debit and refill events show token accounting skew when connections migrate between origin IPs.

Investigation notes so far:
- Hypothesis A: nginx affinity caused stickiness to origin pods that had stale token refill state (sidecar sync lag), causing double-counting or missed refills when sessions moved.
- Hypothesis B: priority-label migration changed route weights so that certain route-level buckets were over-allocated while tenant-level smoothing assumed different proportions, exposing a corner-case in refill alignment logic.
- We reproduced locally by simulating connection handoff between two origin replicas and saw a transient window where requests were rejected until the refill reconciliation kicked in (~18-25s).
- Related PR in rate-limiter repo adds additional reconciliation on origin start (PR referenced above) but does not fully address cross-origin handoff accounting race.

Workarounds provided to customer:
- Revert nginx affinity to round-robin for the dedicated pool as temporary mitigation.
- Stagger batch embedding uploads and websocket session ramp-ups by adding a 10s jitter on worker start.
- Temporarily pin heavy interactive routes to a separate priority-lane configured with an isolated burst pool.

Next steps planned:
1) Engineering to triage rate-limiter origin reconciliation logic and add faster handoff reconciliation (SRE/Serving runtime pairing).
2) Add a canary config to new refill reconciliation in staging and run the customer's choreographed test.
3) Update runbook and console alerting to show per-origin refill drift so we can detect earlier.
4) Postmortem and follow-up ticket for improving rollout guidance when changing priority labels and proxy affinity together.

Customer severity: Customer reports feature impact in production but has an acceptable workaround; we set P1/Sev1 due to user-facing errors.
